bottleneck: Engineered bacteriophages could kill antibiotic-resistant bacteria with precision, but phages evolve, exchange genes, and provoke bacterial resistance of their own. Manufacturing consistent phage cocktails at clinical grade is difficult, dosing pharmacology for a self-replicating agent is poorly understood, and regulators have no established pathway for a drug that mutates. Each patient's infection may need a custom phage, which breaks the one-drug-fits-all regulatory model entirely.
current_state: Compassionate-use phage therapy has saved individual patients. Clinical trials are underway but the personalized-manufacturing model clashes with conventional drug regulation at every step.
title: Engineered phage therapy lacks a regulatory path
why_it_blocks: Antibiotic resistance kills millions yearly while a precision alternative exists in principle. Without frameworks for evolving, personalized biologics, phage therapy stays a last-resort exception instead of a frontline weapon.
